questions.text: How are people, public policy, and support services shaping the e-commerce framework? How can organizations adapt e-distribution and e-procurement to make their B2B transactions better?
questions.html: How are people, public policy, and support services shaping the e-commerce framework? How can organizations adapt e-distribution and e-procurement to make their B2B transactions better?
questions.answerHtml:
An e-commerce framework is the structure of pillars that supports online business, and people, public policy and support services decide how well that structure works in practice.

a) People: People are the direct or indirect users of e-commerce. They may take the merchant side, the customer side, or work as intermediaries, and the system specialists and employees who build and run the site also belong to this pillar. Buyers, sellers and intermediaries connect through the site, so the models (B2C, C2C and others) and the services on offer are designed around who the participants are and what they need.

b) Public policy: Public policy covers the legal issues of the government and its regulating strategy, such as taxation, other laws and the privacy act. It also covers the merchant’s own legal issues, such as terms and conditions, copyrights and trademarks. These rules are needed because online transactions carry risks such as data breaches, identity theft and misuse of personal information. In the framework diagram, public policy, legal and privacy issues stand beside every layer and application, so they limit and protect everything built on top. In Nepal, the Electronic Transaction Act gives legal recognition to online transactions.

c) Support services: Support services are the additional services that keep an e-commerce site running, such as after-sales support, payment gateway services and content services. In daily operation this means several payment options with fraud checking, order tracking and delivery management, and customer accounts. A Nepali shop that accepts e-Sewa or Khalti payments, for instance, depends on a payment gateway service to complete its orders.

Second Part:

An e-distributor is a company that supplies products and services directly to individual businesses. It is owned by one company that seeks to serve many customers. E-procurement is the process of finding, agreeing to terms and acquiring goods or services online. Organizations can adapt both in the following ways:

a) Wider catalog for e-distribution: The more products and services a company makes available on its site, the more attractive the site is to business customers. A distributor should therefore keep a wide and updated catalog on one site.

b) One site for many customers: Since an e-distributor serves many customers from one company, the site should handle repeat orders, prices and delivery for all of them without separate manual work.

c) Electronic document exchange: Both sides should use Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) for purchase orders, invoices, shipping requests and acknowledgements. EDI reduces the cost, delays and errors of manual paper exchange and needs no human intervention.

d) Right price, quality and quantity in procurement: E-procurement helps the buyer decide the market value of the product being purchased. The buyer should compare suppliers online against the right price, timely delivery, right quality and right quantity.

e) Shared visibility: A private industrial network lets suppliers monitor sales, shipment status and inventory levels, as Walmart’s network does for its suppliers. This helps a distributor deliver on time and helps a buyer plan stock.

f) Choosing the right market: For direct production inputs and short-term spot purchasing, a buyer can use an exchange market. For one industry, such as the automobile or chemical industry, an industry consortium marketplace can be used.

questions.text: How does e-cheque work? Consider you are planning for an e-commerce startup facilitating an auctioning service. Explain the possible types of auctioning mechanisms with their use cases that you can facilitate in your platform.
questions.html: How does e-cheque work? Consider you are planning for an e-commerce startup facilitating an auctioning service. Explain the possible types of auctioning mechanisms with their use cases that you can facilitate in your platform.
questions.answerHtml:
An e-cheque is an electronic document that is used instead of a physical cheque for online transactions. It works in the following steps:

a) Creation: The payer fills in the e-cheque details, mainly the amount and the payee, in an electronic form and submits it to the bank.

b) Digital signature: The payer signs the e-cheque with a digital signature. This authenticates the cheque, because only the payer holds the private key used to sign it.

c) Verification through PKI: The bank checks the digital signature and the certificate with the public key infrastructure, which guarantees that the sender is the person who claims to be the payer.

d) Fund check and processing: The bank verifies that the payer’s account has enough funds and then processes the transaction, moving the amount to the payee’s account.

e) Result: Unlike a physical cheque, an e-cheque has no chance of rejection for an authenticity issue. Since PKI is used, there is almost zero chance of fraud.

Second Part:

Auctioning is the process of selling assets, natural resources or other goods through online competitive bidding in an online marketplace. It can take place between businesses, between a business and a consumer, or between consumers, and it is used as a price discovery mechanism when the seller does not know the actual price of an asset. The mechanisms I would offer on my platform are as follows:

a) English auction: The opening price is low and the price keeps rising as bidders bid. It is a public ascending-price auction, a single unit is sold, and the highest bidder wins, so the seller gets the highest possible price. The use case is when the seller is unaware of the price of the item, for example a used phone listed by a consumer on a C2C page like OLX.

b) Dutch auction: It works opposite to the English auction. The seller starts with a high opening price and keeps lowering it until a buyer bids, and the first bidder wins. Single or multiple units can be sold. The use case is when the seller has an expected price for the asset, for example clearing a lot of stock at a price the seller already has in mind.

c) Double auction: Buyers place bids and sellers place offers throughout the trading day. The seller starts with a higher price and the bidder starts with a lower price, and the first match wins. Single or multiple units can be sold. The use case is when there are multiple sellers and multiple bidders, as in the share market.

d) Vickery auction: This is a sealed-bid auction. Bidders submit written bids without knowing the bids of the others, and the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid. Because the winner pays the second-highest bid, bidders have no reason to bid below their true value. The use case is when bids must stay confidential, such as tenders for construction projects.

e) Platform coverage: All these mechanisms can run for B2B, B2C and C2C sales on the platform. Bidders can take part virtually from any part of the world, which gives the sellers competitive value for their assets.

questions.text: How are digital signatures used in e-commerce security? How often are social engineering attacks vulnerable to e-commerce? Being an e-commerce security expert, how can you combat social engineering attacks?
questions.html: How are digital signatures used in e-commerce security? How often are social engineering attacks vulnerable to e-commerce? Being an e-commerce security expert, how can you combat social engineering attacks?
questions.answerHtml:
A digital signature is a close parallel to a handwritten signature. It is created by encrypting the message, or its hash digest, with the sender’s private key, and it can be sent over the Internet along with the message. It is used in e-commerce security in the following ways:

a) Authenticity: The signature proves who sent the message. The receiver checks it with the sender’s public key, so a person who falsely claims to be someone else, for example an order sent by a spoofer, is detected.

b) Non-repudiation: Only one person possesses the private key, so the signer cannot later deny an order, payment or message that carries the signature.

c) Uniqueness and integrity: Used together with a hash function, the signature is even more unique than a handwritten one. Any change to the message in transit changes its digest, so the signature no longer matches and the tampering is exposed.

d) Authentication through PKI: Digital signatures work together with certificates of authority and the public key infrastructure (PKI), which guarantee that the public key really belongs to the claimed sender.

Second Part:

Social engineering is a broad range of malicious activities carried out through human interaction. It uses psychological manipulation to trick users into making security mistakes or giving away sensitive information. Your notes list it among the most common and most damaging threats to e-commerce consumers and site operators.

a) Involvement in breaches: The human element is involved in roughly 60 percent of data breaches, and social engineering is among the top three breach patterns in almost every industry. In retail, system intrusion, social engineering and basic web application attacks together account for 93 percent of breaches.

b) Why the attacks are so frequent: They target people instead of technology, and they exploit trust, lack of awareness, fear of non-compliance and the wish to be helpful. They are also simple and cheap to carry out.

c) Common forms in e-commerce: The techniques include baiting, scareware, pretexting, phishing and spear phishing. A typical case is a fake message that asks a customer for card details or an e-Sewa OTP.

d) Difficulty of defence: No single policy or software gives total protection, so these attacks keep recurring.

Third Part:

As a security expert, I would combine technical controls with people-focused measures:

a) Email and attachment caution: Do not open emails and attachments from suspicious sources. Check for mismatched sender domains, suspicious links and unexpected attachments before acting.

b) Multi-factor authentication: Enforce it on customer, staff and admin accounts, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

c) Updated antivirus software: Keep antivirus and operating system software up to date so that malware delivered through a trick is caught.

d) Employee and customer awareness: Train staff regularly on phishing, pretexting and baiting, and run simulated attacks to test them.

e) Verification protocols: Verify any unusual request for money, passwords or data through a second, official channel before acting on it.

f) Email filters and least privilege: Use anti-phishing and email filtering tools, and give each user only the access they need, which limits the damage if one account is tricked.

g) Reporting and incident response: Report phishing scams immediately, and keep a formal incident response plan, with periodic audits and penetration tests.

questions.text: How are provisions relating to the Information Technology Tribunal defined in the Electronic Transaction Act of Nepal?
questions.html: How are provisions relating to the Information Technology Tribunal defined in the Electronic Transaction Act of Nepal?
questions.answerHtml:
The Information Technology Tribunal is the special body set up under the Electronic Transactions Act of Nepal to hear computer-related offences. Chapter 10 of the Act covers it, and the Chapter 11 provisions on the Appellate Tribunal begin at section 66.

The main provisions are as follows:

a) Formation (section 60): The Government of Nepal forms a Tribunal of three members, one each from law, information technology and commerce. The law member is the chairperson. The Tribunal hears and decides cases on computer-related offences listed in Chapter 9 of the Act, the chapter on computer crimes and punishments.

b) Qualifications of members (section 61): The law member must have knowledge of information technology and be qualified to be a District Court judge. The IT member must be a Nepali citizen with at least a master’s degree in computer science or information technology and three years of experience in electronic transactions or IT. The commerce member must hold a master’s degree in management or commerce, specialising in electronic transactions, with three years of relevant experience.

c) Tenure and service (section 62): Members serve for five years and can be reappointed. Their remuneration and service conditions are set by rules, and they take an oath before the Chief Judge of the Appellate Court.

d) Vacancy of office (section 63): A member’s post falls vacant when the term ends, the member reaches the age of 63, dies or resigns, is convicted of a crime involving moral turpitude, or is removed for proven misbehaviour or incompetence after an inquiry.

e) Procedure (section 65): While starting proceedings and deciding a case under section 60, the Tribunal follows the procedures prescribed by the rules.

f) Appeal (section 60(4)): A person aggrieved by an order or decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within thirty-five days of the order or decision. The Appellate Tribunal has the same three-member structure of law, IT and commerce members and is chaired by the law member.

questions.text: Explain the types of private industrial networks with examples.
questions.html: Explain the types of private industrial networks with examples.
questions.answerHtml:
A private industrial network is a digital network, usually but not always Internet-based, designed to coordinate the flow of communications among firms engaged in business together. It is owned by a large purchasing firm and makes up about 75 percent of all B2B expenditure.

Its two types are as follows:

a) Single-firm network: This is the most common type. One large firm owns and controls the network, and it uses it to coordinate with its own suppliers and distributors. They share information such as sales, shipments, inventory and production scheduling, and the firm and its partners work together as a team.

b) Industry-wide network: This type often grows out of an industry association. It is not owned by one firm but is shared by many firms of the same industry or sector, who all use the same network to coordinate their communication.

Examples

a) Single-firm network: Walmart operates one of the largest private industrial networks in the world for its suppliers. Every day the suppliers use it to monitor the sales of their goods, the status of shipments and the actual inventory level of their goods.

b) Industry-wide network: Agentrics is a network of this kind in the retail industry. It was set up by large retailers and offers e-sourcing and supply chain collaboration tools to retailers such as Tesco and Sainsbury’s and their suppliers.

questions.text: What is the SET protocol? Explain its participants.
questions.html: What is the SET protocol? Explain its participants.
questions.answerHtml:
The Secure Electronic Transaction (SET) protocol is a communication protocol designed for secure electronic payment, such as a credit card transaction, over an open network. It is open source and based on cryptography. SET is not a payment system by itself. It makes the payment transaction safe on an open network by using encryption and hashing, so that hackers cannot get the credit card details.

The participants in the SET protocol are as follows:

a) Cardholder: This is an authorized holder of a payment card, such as a MasterCard or Visa credit card, that has been issued by an issuer.

b) Merchant: This is the seller organization that provides the credit card purchase facility to cardholders. A merchant that accepts credit card payment must have a relationship with an acquirer.

c) Issuer: This is a financial institution, such as a bank, that provides the cardholder with the payment card.

d) Acquirer: This is a financial institution, such as a bank, that keeps the account of the merchant and processes credit card authorization and payments.

e) Certificate authority: This is an entity that provides X.509V3 public-key certificates to cardholders, merchants and payment gateways. These certificates are used to verify who is taking part in the transaction.

f) Payment gateway: This is the system through which the merchant is connected to the payment system. It acts as an interface between the merchant’s website and the payment processing bank.

questions.text: Explain the development of e-commerce websites.
questions.html: Explain the development of e-commerce websites.
questions.answerHtml:
The development of an e-commerce website needs a proper plan and vision before the actual building starts. Once the plan is ready, a plan document is created and the work proceeds step by step through a systems development life cycle (SDLC). The development goes as follows:

a) Planning: A plan is made before building the website or software. The two fundamentals of planning are the timeline and the budget.

b) Vision: There must also be a clear vision for the website. The vision includes the problem statement and the SDLC to be followed.

c) Factors to consider: Once the plan and vision are ready, building and implementation can be thought of. The factors to consider while developing the e-commerce presence are management, software, hardware architecture, design, telecommunications and human resources.

d) System analysis and planning: This stage checks whether the project is technically, financially and operationally feasible, and the requirements of the website are gathered and documented.

e) System design: The agreed requirements are turned into a technical blueprint, covering the architecture of the website and the details of its components, such as the catalog, shopping cart and payment pages.

f) Building the system: Developers build the website according to the approved design, using programming, database and payment gateway integration.

g) Testing: The website is tested to ensure that it meets the requirements and is free from defects before release.

h) Implementation: The tested website is released to users, and it is kept running through support and updates afterwards.

questions.text: What is non-repudiation? Which security mechanism can be used to ensure it? List the threats in E-commerce.
questions.html: What is non-repudiation? Which security mechanism can be used to ensure it? List the threats in E-commerce.
questions.answerHtml:
Non-repudiation:- The ability to ensure that e-commerce participants cannot deny their own online actions is known as non-repudiation. Repudiation means denying one’s own action. For instance, a person can send a message or place an order and later claim that he or she never did so.

Security mechanism for non-repudiation

A digital signature is the mechanism used to ensure non-repudiation. It works as follows:

a) Signing with the private key: The sender encrypts the message, or the hash digest of the message, with his or her own private key. This produces a digital signature that is sent over the Internet along with the message.

b) Uniqueness: Like a handwritten signature, a digital signature is unique, because only one person possesses the private key. Used together with a hash function, it is even more unique than a handwritten signature.

c) Verification and proof: The receiver verifies the signature with the sender’s public key. Since only the private key holder could have created it, the sender cannot later deny having sent the message. This also confirms the authenticity of the message.

d) Support from public key cryptography: Public key (asymmetric) cryptography provides confidentiality, authenticity and non-repudiation, so digital signatures rest on it.

Threats in e-commerce

a) Malicious code (malware): Unwanted programs such as viruses, trojan horses, worms and ransomware that harm a computer or compromise the data stored on it.

b) Adware: Unwanted software, also called a potentially unwanted program (PUP), that throws advertisements on the web browser. It mostly comes with cracked or illegal versions of software.

c) Spyware: Malware installed on a device without the user’s knowledge. It steals sensitive information and Internet usage data.

d) Social engineering: Psychological manipulation of users, through techniques such as baiting, scareware, pretexting and phishing, to make them commit security mistakes or give away sensitive information.

e) Phishing: An attack that tricks users into revealing credit card numbers, bank information or passwords on websites that pretend to be legitimate.

Non-repudiation:- The ability to ensure that e-commerce participants cannot deny their own online actions is known as non-repudiation. Repudiation means denying one’s own action. For instance, a person can send a message or place an order and later claim that he or she never did so.

Security mechanism for non-repudiation

A digital signature is the mechanism used to ensure non-repudiation. It works as follows:

a) Signing with the private key: The sender encrypts the message, or the hash digest of the message, with his or her own private key. This produces a digital signature that is sent over the Internet along with the message.

b) Uniqueness: Like a handwritten signature, a digital signature is unique, because only one person possesses the private key. Used together with a hash function, it is even more unique than a handwritten signature.

c) Verification and proof: The receiver verifies the signature with the sender’s public key. Since only the private key holder could have created it, the sender cannot later deny having sent the message. This also confirms the authenticity of the message.

d) Support from public key cryptography: Public key (asymmetric) cryptography provides confidentiality, authenticity and non-repudiation, so digital signatures rest on it.

Threats in e-commerce

a) Malicious code (malware): Unwanted programs such as viruses, trojan horses, worms and ransomware that harm a computer or compromise the data stored on it.

b) Adware: Unwanted software, also called a potentially unwanted program (PUP), that throws advertisements on the web browser. It mostly comes with cracked or illegal versions of software.

c) Spyware: Malware installed on a device without the user’s knowledge. It steals sensitive information and Internet usage data.

d) Social engineering: Psychological manipulation of users, through techniques such as baiting, scareware, pretexting and phishing, to make them commit security mistakes or give away sensitive information.

e) Phishing: An attack that tricks users into revealing credit card numbers, bank information or passwords on websites that pretend to be legitimate.

f) Hacking: Unauthorized access to a computer system or website by a hacker who finds weaknesses in its security procedures.

g) Credit card fraud and identity theft: Misuse of a victim’s credit card information, or of personal details such as bank account number, address and birth date, for economic gain.

h) Spoofing and pharming: Spoofing is mimicking another person or organization to gather personal or business information. Pharming uses a fake website that resembles a legitimate one to collect usernames and passwords.

questions.text: What is the cost per thousand (CPM)? How is the effective cost per thousand (eCPM) metric used to measure return on investment from a digital ad?
questions.html: What is the cost per thousand (CPM)? How is the effective cost per thousand (eCPM) metric used to measure return on investment from a digital ad?
questions.answerHtml:
The price an advertiser pays for one thousand impressions of an ad is called the cost per thousand (CPM), also written as cost per mille. An impression is one time an ad is served. CPM is calculated as (total campaign cost ÷ total impressions) × 1000, and it is mostly used for banner and other display ads. For example, if a campaign costs Rs 10,000 and gets 500,000 impressions, the CPM is Rs 20.

Use of eCPM to measure return on investment

The effective cost per thousand (eCPM) is the revenue generated per one thousand impressions of an ad. It converts the results of any ad into one common per-thousand-impressions figure. It is used as follows:

a) Calculation: eCPM = (total earnings ÷ total impressions) × 1000. The earnings are the revenue the ads actually produced, whether it came from clicks, sales or direct impression payments.

b) Common yardstick: Ads are sold on different pricing models, such as per impression, per click or per action. Converting each of them into earnings per thousand impressions allows banner ads, video ads and different websites to be compared on the same basis.

c) Measuring return: The eCPM is compared with the CPM actually paid. If the eCPM is higher than the CPM, each thousand impressions returns more than it costs, so the ad gives a positive return on investment.

Example:

Given,
Revenue earned from the ad = Rs 25,000
Impressions = 500,000
Cost of the campaign = Rs 10,000
We know that,
eCPM = (Total earnings ÷ Total impressions) × 1000
or, eCPM = (25,000 ÷ 500,000) × 1000
or, eCPM = Rs 50
CPM = (10,000 ÷ 500,000) × 1000 = Rs 20
ROI = (Revenue − Cost) ÷ Cost = (25,000 − 10,000) ÷ 10,000 = 150%
Hence, the ad earns Rs 50 per thousand impressions against a cost of Rs 20, giving a return of 150 percent.

d) Budget decisions: The advertiser moves the budget to the placements, formats or networks with the higher eCPM and stops those with a low one. A publisher uses the same figure to compare ad networks and to set minimum ad prices.

e) Limitation: eCPM looks only at the revenue per impression. It does not capture brand awareness or the long-term value of a customer, so it is read together with metrics such as click-through rate and conversion rate.

questions.text: How are reach, loyalty, and hits used in display ad marketing metrics?
questions.html: How are reach, loyalty, and hits used in display ad marketing metrics?
questions.answerHtml:
Marketing metrics describe the impact and results of traditional online marketing such as display ads and e-mail campaigns, and display ad marketing metrics such as hits, reach and loyalty tell a business whether its ads are actually bringing in the right visitors. They are used as follows:

a) Hits: A hit is one HTTP request made to the web server. Every request for a page, an image or a script counts as one hit, so counting hits shows how much traffic and load a display ad campaign sends to the site.

b) Limitation of hits: One page with many images produces many hits, so hits alone overstate the audience. They are therefore read together with page views and unique visitors, which count pages viewed and different people in a period.

c) Reach: Reach is the percentage of website visitors who are potential buyers. If a banner ad for a Daraz sale brings many visitors but few of them are potential buyers, the reach is low, and the advertiser should change the ad placement or targeting.

d) Loyalty: Loyalty shows how strongly visitors stay attached to the site. It is measured by the number of page views, how often people return to the website, and the duration of their visits. High loyalty means the ad brought visitors who keep coming back, which matches the e-marketing objective of building loyalty, trust and brand awareness.

e) Combined use with other metrics: Impressions (times the ad is served), click-through rate (percentage of times the ad is clicked) and conversion rate (percentage of visitors who become customers) are studied along with hits, reach and loyalty. They show how well the ad moves a visitor from seeing it to buying.

f) Decision making: The business compares these figures with the ad cost to decide which ads, sites and pricing models to continue, change or stop.

questions.text: What is the significance of page rank in search engine optimization? How can you increase the page rank of an e-commerce website?
questions.html: What is the significance of page rank in search engine optimization? How can you increase the page rank of an e-commerce website?
questions.answerHtml:
PageRank (PR) is an algorithm used by the Google search engine to rank web pages in its search results. It is named after Larry Page, one of the founders of Google. Its significance in search engine optimization is as follows:

a) Measure of importance: PageRank measures the importance of a website’s pages. A page with a higher importance is placed higher in the search results, which is exactly what SEO tries to achieve.

b) Counting links: Google says it works by counting the number and quality of links to a page to estimate how important the website is. The assumption is that more important websites receive more links from other websites. This makes the links pointing to a site (backlinks) a major target of SEO work.

c) Visibility and sales: A good rank puts the site among the first listings, so potential customers find it easily and the return on the web marketing investment improves.

d) Place among ranking factors: PageRank is the first algorithm Google used and the best known, but it is not the only one Google uses to order results. SEO therefore uses it together with on-page work such as content and keywords.

Increasing the page rank of an e-commerce website

a) Diversify the backlink portfolio: Get links from varied and authoritative sites in a natural way, for example from fashion blogs or review sites for an online clothing shop, and avoid outdated spam tactics. A varied portfolio tells Google that the site is an authoritative source.

b) Off-page SEO: Promote the site through link building, influencer outreach, social media engagement, social bookmarking, forum submission and article submission, and keep a Google Business Profile.

c) Quality content and keywords: Do keyword research and build a content strategy around the findings, with the keywords placed in the right places and a suitable title for every product page. Do not stuff pages with keywords.

d) Internal linking and page optimization: Link the pages of the site properly, use clean URLs and keep the navigation clear. Revisit and improve the pages that are not doing well.

e) Technical quality: Make the site mobile-friendly, reduce the load time, and use small image files with alt text for every image.

f) Track the results: Use Google Analytics to study the site’s performance and audience, and track the results of the SEO strategy to see what works and what does not.

questions.text: Consider you are hired as a SEO expert. How can you use content-based and collaborative filtering approaches to recommend products?
questions.html: Consider you are hired as a SEO expert. How can you use content-based and collaborative filtering approaches to recommend products?
questions.answerHtml:
A recommendation system uses algorithms, data analysis and AI to find similar items and similar customers from their behaviour and interests, and then recommends products they are likely to want. Content-based filtering and collaborative filtering are its two main types, and I would use them on the shop as follows:

a) Data collected: Both approaches work on the information that shows user preference: ratings given to a product, search queries made by the user, and the user’s purchase history.

b) Content-based filtering: This approach recommends products using the features of the items a user has liked and the user’s profile. Each product is described by its features (category, brand, colour, price, keywords), and items with similar features are grouped together. If a customer buys a T-shirt on the site, the next visit shows other T-shirts and similar clothing items.

c) Building the user profile: For content-based filtering, the user profile is built from historical interactions such as clicks and purchases, or by asking users directly about their interests. A new product is then matched with this profile, and similarity is usually measured with cosine similarity between the product’s feature vector and the profile.

d) Collaborative filtering: This approach does not need product features. It uses the interactions of many users (ratings, clicks, purchases) to filter items of interest. Netflix and YouTube use it, and it usually gives better results than content-based recommendations.

e) Working of collaborative filtering: In the user-based form, products liked by users with similar behaviour are recommended to the customer. In the item-based form, products that are often bought together with an item the customer already chose are recommended. For example, if two Daraz customers have bought the same phones and one of them also bought a cover, the cover is recommended to the other.

f) Combining the two: Content-based filtering helps with a new product that has no buying history, and collaborative filtering gives varied suggestions beyond the items the customer already knows. Using both together in a hybrid system overcomes the weakness of each.

g) Benefits to the business: Personalized offers increase sales. Users find items of interest faster, and customers are more likely to buy additional products. The company can also gain and retain customers by sending emails with links to new offers that match their interests.

questions.text: What is a dual signature? Describe the dual signature operations? How is dual signature used during purchase request operation of SET protocol?
questions.html: What is a dual signature? Describe the dual signature operations? How is dual signature used during purchase request operation of SET protocol?
questions.answerHtml:
Digital signature is unique, just like a handwritten one, because the private key is only in the possession of one individual. It is a close parallel to a handwritten signature. When used with a hash function, the digital signature is even more unique than a handwritten signature. To ensure the authenticity of the message, and to ensure nonrepudiation, the sender encrypts the entire block of cipher text one or more time using sender’s private key. This produces a digital signature that can be sent over the internet.

In operation of dual signature private and public keys are generated by the involved parties, who are the merchant and the client. Using their respective private keys, the buyer and seller digitally sign their portions of the transaction. A single dual signature is created by fusing the signatures of the client and the merchant. This composite signature is then used to confirm the transaction’s integrity and legitimacy. It can be explained in steps as:

  • Key Generation: A public key and a private key are created by the sender and the recipient.
  • Signing: The sender uses their private key to sign the communication. By doing this, a digital signature is produced that can only be validated with the public key of the sender.
  • Encryption: Using the recipient’s public key, the sender encrypts the message. This guarantees that the communication can only be decrypted by the recipient.
  • Transmission: The recipient receives the encrypted and signed message.
  • Verification: The communication is decrypted by the recipient using their private key. Next, the recipient uses the sender’s public key to confirm the digital signature.

The Secure Electronic Transaction (SET) protocol uses dual signatures to ensure the authenticity and integrity of purchase requests. The customer’s bank uses a dual signature to both sign and encrypt the purchase request. This ensures that the purchase request hasn’t been altered and that the merchant can verify the customer’s identity.

  • The dual signature guarantees that the Order Information (OI) and Payment Information (PI) are connected and unaltered.
  • It is used to authenticate and verify the identity of the merchant and customer.
  • It guarantees the confidentiality of the transaction information, as only the merchant and customer can decrypt the data.
  • The dual signature is used by the payment gateway to confirm the payment details.
  • It ensures that the transaction data is not altered during transmission.

questions.text: What is digital marketing? Why is it essential in e-commerce? How do marketing metrics like click-through rate, bounce-back rate and conversion rate influence E-mail marketing?
questions.html: What is digital marketing? Why is it essential in e-commerce? How do marketing metrics like click-through rate, bounce-back rate and conversion rate influence E-mail marketing?
questions.answerHtml:
Digital marketing is the component of marketing that utilizes internet and online based digital technologies such as desktop computers, mobile phones, and other digital media and platforms to promote products and services. Digital marketing uses a range of strategies to reach customers, to convince customers to reach to products and services or convince them into making a purchase. Modern digital marketing comprises a broad system of channels including: Social media, Content marketing, Website marketing, SEO etc.

It is essential in e-commerce due to following reasons:

  • Understanding the Audience: Aids in comprehending and successfully establishing a connection with the target audience.
  • Cost-Effective: Compared to conventional marketing techniques, it provides an affordable means of reaching a big audience.
  • Reach Worldwide: Enables companies to advertise their goods and services to everyone, anywhere in the globe.
  • Adaptability: Able to quickly adjust to shifting consumer preferences and market trends.
  • Personalization: Gives companies the ability to tailor marketing messages to specific clients via social media, email, and search engines.

Click-through Rate (CTR) measures how many people click on the links in your email. For example, if you send an email to 100 people and 10 click on the product link, your CTR is 10%. A higher CTR means that the email content is engaging, and people are interested in checking out your products. This drives traffic to your website.

Bounce-back Rate refers to how many emails couldn’t be delivered. For example, if 5 out of 100 emails didn’t reach their inboxes, the bounce rate is 5%. A low bounce rate indicates that your email list is clean and accurate. If the rate is high, it could mean you have invalid or spammy email addresses in your list. This helps ensure your messages are reaching potential customers and verifies that your recipients are legitimate.

Conversion Rate is the percentage of email recipients who complete a desired action, such as making a purchase. If 100 people open your email and 5 buy your product, the conversion rate is 5%. This metric shows how effectively your email is driving sales. If the conversion rate is low, adjustments may be needed to make the email more compelling. A higher conversion rate indicates that your email marketing is successful in turning engagement into actual sales.

questions.text: What is B 2 B e-commerce? Discuss various B 2 B business models.
questions.html: What is B 2 B e-commerce? Discuss various B 2 B business models.
questions.answerHtml:
Business-to-business e-commerce is the procedure for locating and accepting terms for the purchase of products or services. It facilitates the purchase of a business. One of the most important aspects of procurement is getting the proper amount, quality, pricing, and delivery time.

Various B 2 B business models are:

1. Network Market Places: Network market places are the online market places where different business vendors can gather and do transaction.

    • E-distributor: Companies that supply products and services directly to individual businesses are distributors. E-distributors are owned by one company seeking to serve many customers. With more products and services a company makes available on it’s site, the more attractive that site is to potential customers.
    • E-Procurement: Procurement is the process of finding and agreeing to terms, and acquiring goods or services. It helps in buying to decide market value of the product or service being purchased by a company. Right price, timely delivery, right quality, right quantity, etc. are major components of procurement.
    • Exchange market: An exchange market is an independent digital marketplace where hundreds of suppliers meet a smaller number of very large commercial purchasers. They focus on the exchange of direct inputs to production and short-term contracts or spot purchasing.
    • Industry consortium: These are industry-owned vertical marketplaces that serve specific industries, such as the automobile, aerospace, chemical etc.

2. Private Industrial Networks: A private industrial network is a digital network designed to coordinate the flow of communications among firms engaged in business together. The network is owned by a single large purchasing firm. It constitutes about 75% of all B2B expenditures. For instance, Walmart operates one of the largest private industrial networks in the world for its suppliers, who on a daily basis use Walmart’s network to monitor the sales of their goods, the status of shipments, and the actual inventory level of their goods.

2. Private Industrial Networks: A private industrial network is a digital network designed to coordinate the flow of communications among firms engaged in business together. The network is owned by a single large purchasing firm. It constitutes about 75% of all B2B expenditures. For instance, Walmart operates one of the largest private industrial networks in the world for its suppliers, who on a daily basis use Walmart’s network to monitor the sales of their goods, the status of shipments, and the actual inventory level of their goods.

questions.text: What does omni-channel mean in terms of e-commerce presence? Justify with an example
questions.html: What does omni-channel mean in terms of e-commerce presence? Justify with an example
questions.answerHtml:
Omnichannel e-commerce is a unified experience for customers across all digital devices and platforms. This strategy ensures that customers can interact with a brand seamlessly, whether they’re shopping on a website, through a mobile app, via social media, or in physical stores.

For example :
A customer might start browsing for Goldstar shoes on the Daraz mobile app, then switch to the Goldstar website to explore more options, and finally visit a physical Goldstar store in Lagankhel to try them on.

With an omnichannel strategy, Goldstar can track the customer’s activity across these platforms, providing consistent product information, promotions, and recommendations, ensuring a smooth shopping experience at every touchpoint.

This approach helps Goldstar understand the customer journey better and create a more personalized experience, ultimately leading to higher customer engagement and more successful sales strategies.

questions.html: What is an e-payment system? How do online credit card transactions work?
questions.answerHtml:
Electronic payment system (EPS) is a way of paying for goods and services electronically instead of using direct cash or physical cheque. EPS simply means online transaction of values. Online Credit Card Transaction, Online Stored Value Payment System, Digital and Mobile Wallet, E-Checks, Virtual Currency etc. are some of the E-payment systems. New types of purchasing relationships, such as between individuals online and new technologies such as the development of the mobile platform, have created both a need and an opportunity for the development of new payment systems.

Online credit card transactions are processed in much the same way that on-the-spot purchases with the major credit cards, but there are some notable differences. There being no inspection of documents, and the actual goods being purchased never even see the credit card, new types of purchases are also called Cardholder Not Present (CNP) transactions.

questions.text: What are the basic elements to be considered while developing an e-commerce website?
questions.html: What are the basic elements to be considered while developing an e-commerce website?
questions.answerHtml:
A platform that enables companies to offer goods or services to customers directly online is known as an e-commerce website. These websites offer a convenient purchasing experience, handle inventories, and streamline transactions. Basic elements to be considered while developing an e-commerce website:

  • Databases:
    Databases are essential to the creation of e-commerce websites because they store, manage, and retrieve information about goods, clients, orders, and transactions. An outline of the types, structures, and best practices of databases used in e-commerce development is provided here.
  • Application Programs:
    When developing an e-commerce website, various application programs and software components are essential for creating a functional, user-friendly, and secure online shopping experience. These applications can be categorized into several key areas, including front-end development, back-end development, payment processing, inventory management etc.
  • Integration with ERP Systems:
    E-commerce websites and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems must be integrated to streamline corporate processes, increase productivity, and offer a smooth experience for internal teams and customers. ERP integration in e-commerce website development is a complex but essential process that requires careful planning, technical expertise, and a strategic approach.
  • Integration with Payment Gateways:
    A crucial step in the construction of an e-commerce website is integrating payment gateways, which allow companies to safely handle online transactions. In addition to improving customer satisfaction and fostering trust, a well executed payment gateway integration guarantees adherence to security regulations.
  •  CMS (Customer Management System):
    In e-commerce, a customer management system (CMS) is a software program that helps companies manage customer connections, data, and interactions across the course of the customer lifecycle. In order to efficiently manage customer relationships, improve customer experiences, and increase revenues, e-commerce development requires a Customer Management System. Businesses may develop a more individualized and effective purchasing experience that encourages client loyalty and pleasure by utilizing a CMS’s capabilities and connecting them with e-commerce platforms.

questions.text: How cryptography and hash functions are used in e-commerce to ensure security.
questions.html: How cryptography and hash functions are used in e-commerce to ensure security.
questions.answerHtml:
Cryptography is essential in order to protect sensitive data’s secrecy, integrity, and validity during e-commerce transactions.

  • Confidentiality: Sensitive information is shielded from unwanted access during transmission by encryption methods such as symmetric key cryptography (AES) and asymmetric key cryptography (RSA, ECC), which convert it into unintelligible ciphertext.
  • Integrity: Data integrity is confirmed by hash algorithms such as SHA-256, which produce distinct “fingerprints” (hash values) for each piece of data. Any change made to the data will produce a new hash value, making manipulation instantly apparent.
  • Non-repudiation: By combining hash functions and asymmetric cryptography, digital signatures enable parties to verify the legitimacy and provenance of a communication or document, avoiding rejection of acts committed.

Hash Functions in E-Commerce

  • Storage of Passwords: In the event of a data breach, hiding plain-text passwords from prying eyes is prevented by hashing them before keeping them.
  • Transaction validation: It is the process of hashing transactions to assure data integrity and that the transaction details have not been altered.

In conclusion, safe e-commerce activities depend on cryptography and hash functions. They provide confidence and dependability in online transactions, preserve sensitive data, and protect user privacy.

questions.text: What is adware? How is the SSL protocol used in e-commerce?
questions.html: What is adware? How is the SSL protocol used in e-commerce?
questions.answerHtml:
“Advertising-supported software,” or “adware,” is a kind of software that downloads or shows adverts on a computer or mobile device automatically. It can be installed without the user’s express permission and is frequently included with free applications. It is designed to throw advertisements on our web browsers. Some security professionals view it as the PUP (potentially unwanted program).

Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) was created to enable safe communication across a computer network; it has now been substantially superseded by Transport Layer Security (TLS). SSL/TLS is essential in the context of e-commerce for a number of reasons:

  • Data Encryption: The information sent between a user’s browser and the e-commerce server is encrypted using SSL/TLS. This guarantees that bad actors cannot intercept sensitive data while it is being sent, including credit card numbers, personal information, and login credentials.
  • Authentication: SSL/TLS offers a way to confirm that the people communicating are who they say they are. This makes it easier to verify that clients are engaging with trustworthy e-commerce websites rather than phony ones.
  • Data Integrity: SSL/TLS guarantees that no changes were made to the data being delivered or received during transmission. Maintaining the precision and dependability of transactions depends on this.
  • Trust indications: SSL/TLS-enabled websites frequently have trust indications, including “https://” in the URL or a padlock icon in the browser’s address bar. Customers’ trust and confidence in the site’s security are increased by these signs.

In conclusion, SSL/TLS is crucial for safeguarding e-commerce transactions online, shielding the company and its clients from possible security risks.

questions.text: How social marketing, mobile marketing and local marketing are used in e-commerce to promote business.
questions.html: How social marketing, mobile marketing and local marketing are used in e-commerce to promote business.
questions.answerHtml:
Social marketing is a calculated strategy that use marketing concepts and methods to change people’s behavior for the betterment of society. By encouraging people and groups to adopt desirable habits, social marketing seeks to achieve positive social change, in contrast to traditional marketing, which largely focuses on pushing goods or services for profit.

Social marketing in e-commerce promote business in following ways:

  • Engagement and Brand Loyalty: To produce interesting content that appeals to target audiences, social marketers use sites like Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok. This includes community-building and brand-loyalty-promoting interactive postings, tales, and live sessions.
  • Influencer Partnerships: In order to reach a larger audience, brands collaborate with influencers. Influencers build trust with their audience by producing genuine content that highlights products, increasing interest and revenue.
  • Social Commerce: Customers may buy things directly from social media networks without ever leaving the app. The purchasing process is streamlined by features like in-app checkout and shoppable articles.

Mobile marketing refers to the methods and approaches used to connect with and interact with customers via their mobile devices, including tablets and smartphones. E-commerce companies are using mobile marketing more and more to improve consumer experiences, increase sales, and foster brand loyalty as mobile usage keeps growing.

Mobile marketing in e-commerce promote business in following ways:

  • Personalized Advertising: Using data from user activity and preferences, mobile marketing targets consumers with tailored advertisements. Push alerts, SMS marketing, and in-app ads that promote quick action are examples of this.
  • Mobile-Optimized Experiences: It’s critical to make sure websites and online shops are responsive to mobile devices. Conversion rates rise and user engagement is improved with a smooth mobile experience.
  • Location-Based Marketing: In order to increase foot traffic and encourage in-store sales, location-based marketing give consumers personalized advertising when they are close to a physical store.

Local marketing in e-commerce describes methods and approaches used to draw clients to a company’s website or physical location from a particular region. This strategy is especially crucial for companies that operate physically or cater to a specific local market.

Local marketing in e-commerce promote business in following ways:

  • Local marketing draw clients from a particular region. Businesses may send promotions to prospective clients when they reach a designated region by using strategies like geofencing.
  • Creating connections with nearby communities through partnerships, sponsorships, and events may increase brand awareness and adherence.
  • Businesses that optimize their online presence for local search results are more likely to show up in local consumer searches, which increases the possibility that both online and physical stores will draw in local customers.

questions.text: Describe the working mechanism of search engines.
questions.html: Describe the working mechanism of search engines.
questions.answerHtml:
A search engine is a software accessible through a Web site that helps people find things on the Web. Search engines contain three major parts: Spider, Index, and Search utility.

  • Spider:
    It is a program that automatically searches the Web to find Web pages that might be interesting to people. When the spider finds Web pages, it collects the URL of the page and information contained in the page. This information might include the page’s title, keywords included in the pages, and information about other pages on the Web site. The keywords are enclosed in an HTML tag set called meta tags.
  • Index:
    The store element of a search engine is called its index or database. The spider returns information to the index. The index checks to see if information about the Web page is already stored. If it is, it compares the stored information to the new information and determines whether to update the page information. The index is designed to allow fast searches of its very large amount of stored information.
  • Search Utility:
    Search utility takes search items and finds entries for Web pages in its index that match those search terms. The Search utility program creates a Web page that has a list of links to URLs that the search engine has found in its index that match the site visitor’s search terms. The visitor can then click the links to visit those sites.

questions.text: Briefly explain the electronic transaction act of Nepal.
questions.html: Briefly explain the electronic transaction act of Nepal.
questions.answerHtml:
The Electronic Transactions Act of Nepal, enacted in 2008, establishes a legal framework for electronic commerce and digital transactions in the country. Key features include:

  1. Legal Recognition: Grants legal validity to electronic records and digital signatures, equating them with traditional documents and signatures.
  2. Consumer Protection: Ensures consumer rights are protected in electronic transactions, providing access to information about products and services.
  3. Regulatory Authority: Establishes a regulatory body to oversee compliance, issue licenses, and manage electronic transaction standards.
  4. Data Protection: Emphasizes the importance of protecting personal data and privacy in electronic transactions.
  5. Dispute Resolution: Provides mechanisms for resolving disputes related to electronic transactions, including arbitration options.
  6. Penalties: Outlines penalties for violations, such as unauthorized access and misuse of digital signatures.

Overall, the Act aims to promote and regulate the growth of the digital economy in Nepal, enhancing trust in electronic transactions.

questions.text: What is competitive advantage in a business model? How can firms achieve competitive advantage using dimensions of asymmetry, complementary resources, perfect market and leverage?
questions.html: What is competitive advantage in a business model? How can firms achieve competitive advantage using dimensions of asymmetry, complementary resources, perfect market and leverage?
questions.answerHtml:
Competitive advantage in a business model refers to the unique strengths or attributes that enable a company to outperform its competitors in a particular industry or market. It’s essentially what sets a company apart and allows it to create superior value for its customers while generating higher profits.

There are several ways firms can achieve competitive advantage using different dimensions:

  1. Asymmetry: Asymmetry refers to the differences or imbalances between competitors in terms of resources, capabilities, or market positioning. Firms can exploit these differences to gain a competitive edge. For example, a company might have superior technology, intellectual property, or access to exclusive distribution channels that its competitors lack. By leveraging these advantages, the company can offer better products or services, attract more customers, and capture a larger market share.
  2. Complementary resources: Complementary resources are assets or capabilities that, when combined, create greater value or efficiency than when used separately. Firms can achieve competitive advantage by strategically combining their resources with those of partners, suppliers, or other stakeholders. For instance, a manufacturer might collaborate with a technology company to integrate cutting-edge software into its products, enhancing their performance and appeal to customers.
  3. Perfect market: While a perfectly competitive market is theoretical and rarely exists in reality, the concept can still be useful for understanding how firms can achieve competitive advantage. In a perfectly competitive market, firms have no control over prices and must compete solely on factors like product quality, customer service, and brand reputation. To gain a competitive advantage in such a market, firms must focus on differentiating themselves through innovation, efficiency, or other means to attract customers and earn profits.
  4. Leverage: Leverage involves using specific tactics or strategies to amplify the impact of existing resources or capabilities. Firms can achieve competitive advantage by leveraging their strengths in ways that create additional value or opportunities. For example, a company might leverage its strong brand reputation to expand into new markets or diversify its product offerings. Similarly, firms can leverage their financial resources to invest in research and development, marketing campaigns, or acquisitions that enhance their competitive position.

questions.text: What is a digital wallet? How does it work? Describe the payment authorization and payment capture operations of SET.
questions.html: What is a digital wallet? How does it work? Describe the payment authorization and payment capture operations of SET.
questions.answerHtml:
A digital wallet, also known as an e-wallet or mobile wallet, is a software-based system that securely stores users’ payment information, such as credit card details, bank account numbers, or cryptocurrency keys, for making online transactions. Digital wallets can be accessed through various devices, including smartphones, tablets, and computers, and they enable users to make purchases, send money to others, and manage their financial accounts conveniently and securely.

Here’s how a digital wallet typically works:

  1. Registration: Users download a digital wallet application and create an account by providing personal information and linking their preferred payment methods, such as credit/debit cards or bank accounts.
  2. Security: To ensure the security of users’ sensitive information, digital wallets employ encryption techniques and authentication mechanisms like passwords, PINs, biometrics (e.g., fingerprint or facial recognition), or two-factor authentication.
  3. Storage of Payment Information: Once registered, users can securely store their payment information within the digital wallet. This eliminates the need to repeatedly enter payment details for each transaction.
  4. Transaction Initiation: When making a purchase online or in-store, users select the digital wallet as their payment method and authorize the transaction using their chosen authentication method.
  5. Payment Authorization: The digital wallet communicates with the payment processor or financial institution to authorize the transaction. This involves verifying the user’s identity, checking the availability of funds, and ensuring the transaction meets security standards.

questions.text: What is display ad marketing? How attrition rate, view-to-cart ratio, acquisition rate and retention rate influence display ad marketing?
questions.html: What is display ad marketing? How attrition rate, view-to-cart ratio, acquisition rate and retention rate influence display ad marketing?
questions.answerHtml:
Display ad marketing refers to the practice of promoting products, services, or brands through visual advertisements that appear on websites, social media platforms, mobile apps, and other digital channels. These ads typically consist of images, graphics, videos, or interactive elements and are displayed to targeted audiences based on demographics, interests, browsing behavior, and other criteria.

  1. Attrition Rate: Attrition rate refers to the rate at which customers stop engaging with a brand or product over a specific period. In display ad marketing, a high attrition rate indicates that a significant portion of the audience exposed to the ads is not converting or taking desired actions, such as making purchases or signing up for services. Analyzing attrition rate helps marketers identify potential issues with ad creatives, targeting, messaging, or user experience that may be causing audiences to disengage.
  2. View-to-Cart Ratio: The view-to-cart ratio measures the percentage of users who add items to their shopping carts after viewing a display ad. This metric is particularly relevant for e-commerce businesses that use display ads to drive product sales. A high view-to-cart ratio indicates that the ad effectively captures the audience’s interest and motivates them to explore further or take action. Conversely, a low view-to-cart ratio suggests that the ad may not be resonating with the target audience or that there are barriers preventing users from progressing to the next stage of the purchase funnel.
  3. Acquisition Rate: The acquisition rate represents the proportion of users who become new customers or subscribers as a result of interacting with display ads. It measures the effectiveness of display ad campaigns in acquiring new business opportunities or expanding the customer base. A high acquisition rate indicates that the ads are successfully attracting and converting prospects into paying customers or engaged users. Marketers can optimize their campaigns to improve the acquisition rate by refining audience targeting, optimizing ad creatives and messaging, and enhancing the user experience on landing pages or conversion paths.
  4. Retention Rate: Retention rate measures the percentage of customers or users who continue to engage with a brand or product over time. In the context of display ad marketing, retention rate reflects the effectiveness of ongoing campaigns in nurturing existing relationships, encouraging repeat purchases, and fostering brand loyalty. A high retention rate indicates that the ads are resonating with existing customers and reinforcing their affinity for the brand, leading to sustained engagement and repeat business. Marketers can enhance retention rate by delivering personalized ad experiences, offering relevant incentives or promotions, and providing exceptional post-purchase support or customer service.

questions.text: What are some of the factors driving the growth of social e-commerce?
questions.html: What are some of the factors driving the growth of social e-commerce?
questions.answerHtml:
Social e-commerce, the convergence of social media and online shopping, has experienced significant growth in recent years, driven by several key factors:

  1. Increasing Social Media Usage: The widespread adoption of social media platforms globally has provided a fertile ground for social e-commerce to thrive. With billions of users active on platforms like Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Pinterest, businesses have a vast audience to reach and engage with directly.
  2. Social Media Shopping Features: Social media platforms have introduced various shopping features and functionalities to facilitate e-commerce transactions directly within their ecosystems. Features like Instagram Shopping, Facebook Shops, and Pinterest Buyable Pins enable users to discover and purchase products seamlessly without leaving the platform.
  3. Influencer Marketing: Influencer marketing has become a powerful driver of social e-commerce growth. Influencers, who have built large and engaged audiences on social media, can effectively promote products and brands to their followers, driving awareness, consideration, and purchase intent. Many influencers also collaborate with brands through affiliate marketing programs, earning commissions for driving sales.
  4. User-Generated Content (UGC): User-generated content, such as product reviews, ratings, and recommendations shared by consumers on social media, plays a crucial role in influencing purchase decisions. Social e-commerce leverages UGC to build trust, credibility, and social proof, as consumers are more likely to trust recommendations from peers or influencers they follow.
  5. Mobile Commerce: The proliferation of smartphones and mobile devices has made it easier for consumers to shop online anytime, anywhere. Social e-commerce capitalizes on the mobile-first behavior of consumers, offering seamless shopping experiences optimized for mobile platforms, including mobile-friendly websites, apps, and social media integrations.
  6. Personalization and Targeting: Social media platforms collect vast amounts of data about users’ interests, preferences, and behaviors, enabling highly targeted and personalized advertising campaigns. Social e-commerce leverages data-driven insights to deliver relevant product recommendations, advertisements, and content tailored to individual users, increasing the likelihood of conversion and engagement.
  7. Live Commerce and Interactive Experiences: Live commerce, or live streaming shopping, has emerged as a popular trend in social e-commerce, particularly in markets like China. Live streaming allows brands and influencers to showcase products in real-time, interact with viewers, answer questions, and drive immediate purchases, creating engaging and immersive shopping experiences.
  8. Social Proof and FOMO: Social e-commerce leverages psychological triggers like social proof (e.g., testimonials, user-generated content) and fear of missing out (FOMO) to stimulate demand and urgency among consumers. Limited-time offers, exclusive deals, and social validation from peers encourage users to make purchase decisions quickly, driving sales and conversions.

questions.text: What is EDI? Describe the significance of EDI in e-commerce? Justify your answer with an example.
questions.html: What is EDI? Describe the significance of EDI in e-commerce? Justify your answer with an example.
questions.answerHtml:
Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) is the electronic exchange of business documents, such as purchase orders, invoices, shipment notices, and other transactional information, between trading partners in a standardized format.

The significance of EDI in e-commerce lies in its ability to streamline and improve the efficiency, accuracy, and speed of business-to-business (B2B) transactions.

  1. Efficiency: EDI eliminates the need for manual data entry and paper-based processes, reducing the time, effort, and resources required to exchange business documents between trading partners. This increases operational efficiency and enables organizations to process transactions faster, leading to shorter order-to-cash cycles and improved productivity.
  2. Accuracy: By standardizing the format and structure of business documents, EDI reduces the risk of errors, discrepancies, and misinterpretations that can occur with manual data entry or paper-based systems. This improves data accuracy and integrity, minimizing the likelihood of order processing errors, invoicing discrepancies, and other costly mistakes.
  3. Cost Savings: EDI helps businesses save costs by eliminating the need for paper-based document storage, printing, postage, and manual labor associated with document processing. It also reduces the risk of late payments, invoice disputes, and order processing delays, leading to lower operational expenses and improved cash flow management.
  4. Speed and Agility: EDI enables real-time or near-real-time exchange of data between trading partners, allowing businesses to respond quickly to customer demands, market changes, and supply chain disruptions. This agility is essential in today’s fast-paced e-commerce environment, where timely order fulfillment and delivery are critical for customer satisfaction and retention.
  5. Integration with E-commerce Platforms: EDI can be seamlessly integrated with e-commerce platforms, enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, inventory management systems, and other business applications, enabling end-to-end automation and synchronization of data across the entire supply chain. This integration streamlines business processes, enhances visibility, and facilitates better decision-making.

Example: Consider a retailer that sells consumer electronics products through its e-commerce website. The retailer sources products from multiple suppliers and manufacturers located around the world. To streamline its procurement process and manage inventory effectively, the retailer implements an EDI system to exchange purchase orders, shipment notices, and invoices with its suppliers electronically.

When the retailer needs to restock inventory, its inventory management system automatically generates a purchase order in the standardized EDI format and sends it electronically to the suppliers. The suppliers receive the purchase orders instantly, process them electronically, and prepare the requested products for shipment. Once the products are ready to be shipped, the suppliers generate electronic shipment notices (ASN) and send them to the retailer, providing details about the shipment, such as tracking numbers, quantities, and expected delivery dates.

Upon receiving the shipment notices, the retailer’s system automatically updates its inventory records, notifies the warehouse staff to expect incoming shipments, and prepares to receive and process the products upon arrival. When the products are delivered, the retailer receives electronic invoices from the suppliers, which are automatically matched with the corresponding purchase orders and shipment notices to reconcile the transactions.

In this example, EDI enables the retailer and its suppliers to exchange business documents efficiently, accurately, and electronically, leading to streamlined procurement processes, improved inventory management, and faster order fulfillment.

questions.text: What is virtual currency? How does it work? Mention the usages of virtual currency in e-commerce.
questions.html: What is virtual currency? How does it work? Mention the usages of virtual currency in e-commerce.
questions.answerHtml:
Virtual currency, also known as digital currency or cryptocurrency, is a type of digital or electronic currency that exists purely in electronic form and is not backed by any physical commodity or government authority. Virtual currencies are decentralized and typically rely on cryptographic techniques to secure transactions and control the creation of new units.

Here’s how virtual currency works:

  1. Blockchain Technology: Many virtual currencies, such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, are based on blockchain technology. A blockchain is a decentralized, distributed ledger that records all transactions across a network of computers. Each transaction is verified by network participants (miners) and added to a block, which is then linked to previous blocks, creating a chain of blocks (hence the term “blockchain”).
  2. Cryptography: Virtual currencies use cryptographic techniques to secure transactions and control the creation of new units. Public and private keys are used to encrypt and decrypt transaction information, ensuring the security and integrity of the network.
  3. Decentralization: Unlike traditional currencies, which are issued and regulated by governments or central banks, virtual currencies operate in a decentralized manner, meaning they are not controlled by any single authority. Transactions are validated and recorded by network participants, eliminating the need for intermediaries like banks or payment processors.
  4. Mining: Some virtual currencies, such as Bitcoin, use a process called mining to create new units and verify transactions. Miners use powerful computers to solve complex mathematical puzzles, which validate transactions and add them to the blockchain. In return, miners are rewarded with newly created units of the virtual currency.

Usages of virtual currency in e-commerce include:

  1. Payment Method: Virtual currencies can be used as a payment method for purchasing goods and services online. Many e-commerce merchants accept virtual currencies as a form of payment, providing customers with an alternative payment option.
  2. Cross-Border Transactions: Virtual currencies can facilitate cross-border transactions by eliminating the need for currency conversion and reducing transaction fees associated with traditional payment methods. This makes it easier for customers to make purchases from international e-commerce websites.
  3. Lower Transaction Fees: Virtual currency transactions typically have lower transaction fees compared to traditional payment methods like credit cards or bank transfers. This can benefit e-commerce merchants by reducing payment processing costs and increasing profit margins.
  4. Anonymity and Privacy: Virtual currencies offer a certain degree of anonymity and privacy for users, as transactions are pseudonymous and not directly linked to personal identity information. This can appeal to customers who prioritize privacy when making online purchases.
  5. Micropayments: Virtual currencies enable micropayments, allowing users to make small transactions or pay for digital content on a per-use basis. This can be useful for e-commerce platforms that offer digital downloads, subscriptions, or pay-per-view services.

questions.text: What is catalog in e-commerce? How are catalogs created?
questions.html: What is catalog in e-commerce? How are catalogs created?
questions.answerHtml:
In e-commerce, a catalog refers to a digital or online listing or collection of products or services that a retailer or seller offers for sale. It serves as a comprehensive and organized showcase of available items, allowing customers to browse, search, and select products they wish to purchase.

Here’s how catalogs are typically created in e-commerce:

  1. Product Information Gathering: The first step in creating an e-commerce catalog is to gather all the necessary information about the products or services to be included. This may include product names, descriptions, specifications, prices, images, SKUs (stock keeping units), categories, and any other relevant details.
  2. Product Photography and Imaging: High-quality images are essential for showcasing products effectively in an e-commerce catalog. Sellers typically photograph or obtain images of the products from manufacturers, ensuring that they accurately represent the appearance, features, and details of each item.
  3. Content Creation: Once product information and images are collected, sellers create compelling and informative content for each product listing. This may involve writing product descriptions, highlighting key features and benefits, specifying technical specifications, and providing any other relevant details that help customers make informed purchasing decisions.
  4. Catalog Structure and Organization: Sellers organize the products into categories, subcategories, or collections to facilitate navigation and improve the shopping experience for customers. Categories may be based on product type, brand, price range, or any other relevant criteria. A well-structured catalog makes it easier for customers to find the products they’re looking for quickly.
  5. Catalog Software or Platform: Sellers use e-commerce platforms, content management systems (CMS), or specialized catalog management software to create and manage their catalogs. These tools provide features and functionalities for adding, editing, organizing, and updating product listings, as well as managing inventory, pricing, and promotions.
  6. Data Entry and Upload: Sellers input product information, descriptions, prices, and other details into the catalog management system or software. They may also upload product images and multimedia content to enhance product listings. Depending on the platform or software used, sellers may have to follow specific formatting guidelines or templates for data entry and upload.
  7. Quality Assurance and Review: Before publishing the catalog online, sellers typically review and verify each product listing to ensure accuracy, consistency, and completeness. This may involve checking for typos, errors, missing information, broken links, or discrepancies between product descriptions and images.
  8. Publishing and Updates: Once the catalog is finalized and reviewed, sellers publish it on their e-commerce website or platform, making it accessible to customers for browsing and shopping. Sellers regularly update the catalog to add new products, remove discontinued items, adjust prices, or make other changes based on inventory updates, customer feedback, or market trends.
